source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC4547584 (commentary without section headings, 12 running-text paragraphs, the indicator list, the Figure caption and footnotes), read in my own browser tab; no claim number comes from the Figure image

claims.note: The commentary gives the coding chain the claim relies on: the certifier writes the cause; NCHS software codes it; a named opioid analgesic goes to T40.2-T40.4, 'opioid' alone to T40.6, and 'drug overdose' with no drug to T50.9 ('other and unspecified drugs'). It also names X85 'assault', matching the claim. Its recommendation (compare jurisdictions on total overdose rates, not drug-specific ones; drug-specific trends are usable only if specification is stable) bears on the claim's point that figures from different sources do not count the same thing.

anchors.extracted: Certifiers record a drug's role in different ways: a named opioid analgesic (e.g. hydrocodone, methadone, tramadol) is coded in T40.2-T40.4; 'opioid' alone goes to T40.6 'other and unspecified narcotics'; 'drug overdose' with no drug named does not show the opioid at all and is coded T50.9 'other and unspecified drugs'.

Coroners or medical examiners determine the cause and complete the certificate; NCHS codes it with automated software; a drug overdose death has underlying cause X40-X44 (unintentional), X60-X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10-Y14 (undetermined); T36-T50 identify drug classes.

The workgroup judges that ranking jurisdictions by specific drug types from certificates may mislead; comparisons should use total overdose rates; trends in drug-specific rates stay useful while the degree of drug specification does not change markedly from year to year.

claims.overstatement: Clarity: the 9,429 deaths coded only T50.9 are inside the 38,329 overdose total; what they are missing from is drug-specific counts (the authors' concern is undercounting opioid-analgesic and heroin deaths). The claim's opening 'official counts missed some drug deaths ... because the certificate named no drug' should say drug-specific counts for this part. The authors' view that many unspecified deaths were opioid deaths ('possible, even likely') is an inference, not a measured share.
claims.note: 9,429 / 38,329 = 24.6%, so 'about a quarter' is right; the share rests on the commentary's own CDC WONDER query (2010 multiple-cause data: T50.9 with no other code in T36-T50.8). Same paragraph: 16,651 deaths (43.4%) listed an opioid analgesic; earlier work found about 25% of US overdose deaths had no drug specified. State examples: Kansas and Michigan had more deaths coded to unspecified drugs than to opioid analgesics; Oklahoma only 28 (4%).

anchors.extracted: US 2010: 38,329 overdose deaths on death certificates (age-adjusted 12.3/100,000); an opioid analgesic was listed in 16,651 (5.4/100,000); a further 9,429 (3.0/100,000) were associated only with 'other and unspecified drugs' (24.6%, editors' arithmetic); earlier work found about 25% of US overdose deaths had no drug specified, so national statistics likely underestimate opioid-analgesic and heroin deaths by a substantial fraction.

anchors.locator: Indicator list after the 7th paragraph (4th indicator)
anchors.extracted: The 'only other and unspecified drugs' indicator counts overdose deaths with code T50.9 and no other drug-poisoning code in T36-T50.8 (crude rate).

Oklahoma's top opioid-analgesic rate (13.6/100,000) partly reflects few unspecified deaths (28, 4% of its overdose deaths); unspecified-drug rates were high in Kansas (4.2), Michigan (4.8) and Kentucky (7.4); in Kansas and Michigan more deaths were coded to unspecified drugs than to opioid analgesics; the authors think opioid involvement there was likely underestimated.
Nonspecific wording can undercount drug classes; compare jurisdictions on total overdose rates; drug-specific trends are usable only while drug specification is stable.

claims.overstatement: Selective: the commentary (citing Warner et al., 2013) gives four system averages: centralized state medical examiner 92%, hybrid county coroner and medical examiner 73%, decentralized county or district medical examiner 71%, decentralized coroner 62%. Quoting only 92% against 62% presents a centralized-versus-decentralized contrast as a medical-examiner-versus-coroner one; among decentralized systems the gap was 71% against 62%. The 73% and 71% figures belong in the claim, since its question is the type of official.
claims.note: Numbers 92% and 62% confirmed, correctly labelled second-hand ('as cited'). They are state-level averages of the share of overdose certificates listing specific drugs; the commentary gives no year, count or uncertainty for them.

anchors.extracted: Citing earlier work: states with centralized state medical examiner systems averaged 92% of overdose certificates listing specific drugs, against 62% in decentralized coroner systems, 73% in hybrid county coroner and medical examiner systems, and 71% in decentralized county or district medical examiner systems; the authors say underestimation varied with the certification system.
